AI Investors Seek Downside Protection
 
Plus, backlash against continuation deals and states try to slow ‘super speeders’
 
 
JASON HENRY FOR WSJ
 

Wall Street placed a multitrillion-dollar bet on artificial intelligence. Some investors are desperate to take the other side.

 

The trade has proved a lasting winner up to now. Excitement about AI’s potential to transform the economy has lifted stocks from tech heavyweights to utilities and chip makers, while driving a speculative frenzy in other corners of the market.

 

Some of these optimistic forecasts got a recent reality check, with big and small players alike failing to meet the market’s expectations. Now, investors are sizing up how to protect themselves against the risk of a larger unraveling.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

 
 
 

Planning & Investing

 

Private Equity’s Take-It-Or-Leave-It Continuation Deals Frustrate Investors

 

A backlash is growing against continuation vehicles, which can benefit fund managers over their investors.

 
 
 

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Issuance of new U.S. dollar corporate bonds is expected to rise to around $180 billion to $190 billion in November, TD Securities’ Hans Mikkelsen says in a note. New credit issuance is likely to be driven by AI-linked supply and mergers and acquisitions, he says. New U.S. dollar IG supply declined in October to $127 billion, from $196 billion in September, Mikkelsen says. The average duration on new IG bonds was shorter in October due to high interest rates, with just 7.7% of deals coming longer than 10 years, he says. “Expect something similar in November.” (Miriam Mukuru, miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

 

The rise in the October ISM manufacturing survey was partly due to the ongoing AI buildout, according to a note from Capital Economics, while the prices paid index ticked down slightly. “The drop back in the prices paid index was a surprise considering the further leg up in oil prices last month,” analysts say. However, that is hardly a reprieve for the FOMC, as the index remains consistent with headline inflation staying close to 4% around the turn of the year. “This will hardly reassure the Fed that inflation pressures are easing,” the note says. (Jessica Coacci, jessica.coacci@wsj.com)
